0.0.n: The て-form of 見る works alone as a casual request.

0.2.n: This noun refers to things to eat collectively.

0.3.n: Marks 食べ物 as what there is a lot of.

0.4.n: Describes the large amount of food; a verb like ある is left unspoken.

1.0.n: 食べる changes to 食べたい with たい, expressing the speaker’s desire.

1.2.n: Repeating this form emphasizes the speaker’s excitement.

1.4.n: Refers to all the food; the object marker を is omitted in this casual sentence.

1.5.n: The たい ending expresses desire, now directed at all the food.

2.0.n: A polite way to address a group, using the respectful ending さん.

2.2.n: A standard daytime greeting; its final は is pronounced like わ.

3.0.n: Links to the following title through の.

3.1.n: Connects 今日 to the title, identifying today’s installment.

3.3.n: In this segment title, it pairs with 一言 to suggest a daily phrase.

3.4.n: Can mean a word or brief remark; here it names the daily expression.

3.6.n: Marks today’s segment as the topic; the sentence continues in the next line.

4.1.n: This borrowed word means buffet dining in Japanese, not the historical seafarers.

4.3.n: Politely completes the identification begun in the previous line.

5.1.n: The speaker discusses the Japanese word itself, comparing it with ヴァイキング.

5.3.n: Makes バイキング the topic of the comparison.

5.4.n: This is the Japanese name for Europe.

5.5.n: Links Europe to the Vikings, indicating their geographical association.

5.7.n: Refers to the historical Norse seafarers, unlike the dining term バイキング.

5.9.n: Marks what バイキング resembles when used with 似ています.

5.10.n: Polite ている form of 似る describes an existing resemblance, here in sound.

5.11.n: Invites the listener to agree with the comparison.

6.0.n: Introduces a contrast with the similarity just mentioned.

6.2.n: Refers to what the Japanese dining term signifies.

6.3.n: Identifies 意味 as the thing that differs.

6.4.n: Strengthens 違います; 全然 can accompany a positive verb expressing difference.

6.5.n: The polite form of 違う contrasts the meanings of the two words.

6.6.n: Adds emphasis and presents the contrast as information for the listener.

7.0.n: This is the country name, setting the context for the word’s usage.

7.1.n: Marks Japan as the setting where this usage applies.

7.3.n: The Japanese dining term is being explained through 食べ放題.

7.5.n: Marks バイキング as the word being defined.

7.7.n: Combines the stem of 食べる with 放題 to express eating without a quantity limit.

7.9.n: Introduces the explanation; together, ということです says what the term means.

7.10.n: Packages 食べ放題 as the content of the definition in ということです.

8.1.n: The speaker now explains how this dining arrangement works.

8.3.n: Sets 食べ放題 as the topic whose definition continues into the next line.

8.4.n: Specifies that the payment happens one time.

8.5.n: The prefix お is conventional in this everyday noun.

8.6.n: Marks お金 as what is paid.

8.7.n: The ば conditional form of 払う makes payment the condition for eating freely.

9.0.n: Combines with でも to form 何でも, allowing any choice of food.

9.1.n: After 何, it makes 何でも mean anything rather than asking a question.

9.2.n: This quantity word combines with でも to allow any number of items.

9.3.n: After いくつ, it removes a numerical limit: as many as you like.

9.4.n: The ability form of 食べる expresses what the diner is allowed to do here.

9.5.n: Turns the preceding description into a noun-like phrase so it can serve as the definition.

9.6.n: Politely completes the definition that began in the previous line.

0.tip: A て-form alone, like 見て, can make a casual request.

1.lit: Want to eat, want to eat, everything want to eat!
1.tip: Attach たい to the verb stem to express what you want to do.

2.tip: 皆さん is a polite, friendly way to address an audience.

3.lit: As for today’s One Day, One Phrase,
3.tip: は introduces the topic, but its explanation can continue in the next subtitle.

4.tip: バイキング means buffet dining in Japanese, despite its connection to the word Viking.

5.lit: Buffet resembles Europe’s Vikings, doesn’t it?
5.tip: Use と with 似ています to mark the thing something resembles.

6.lit: But the meaning is completely different, I tell you!
6.tip: 全然 works with 違います to emphasize a complete difference, even without a negative ending.

7.tip: ということです can explain what a word or expression means.

8.lit: As for all-you-can-eat, if you pay money once,
8.tip: 払えば uses the ば ending to introduce a condition: if you pay.

9.lit: It is being able to eat anything, any number.
9.tip: A question word followed by でも allows unrestricted choice, as in 何でも and いくつでも.
